academicJudgment.claimTested: UCR offers real Dutch-language foundations, cultural comparison, literary/film/visual interpretation and language-acquisition research. Its strongest feasible cultural and empirical-language combinations do not sustain Dutch society, national history, literature and structural/historical language as the continuing taught academic object. This shortfall remains after allowing translated sources, favorable Dutch research topics and either informal Language or Culture direction; it is not based on missing Dutch proficiency or the degree title alone.
academicJudgment.strongestObjection: A broad LAS programme need not replicate a national degree or advanced Dutch proficiency. UCR provides real beginner Dutch and culture, literature/film/visual interpretation, painting-on-location research, psycholinguistic acquisition/bilingualism, historical source inquiry, local civic work and experimental/qualitative/data methods. Dutch sources or painting topics might be selected in legitimate projects. The corrected curriculum adds generic philosophy/digital-humanities study that UCR can substantially address. These are genuine positive connections and must not be dismissed as generic context.
academicJudgment.finding: Both full feasible challenges preserve those connections, including real Dutch film/music/cultural comparison, actual interpretation and language-research methods and a favorable Dutch painting/topic choice. The known external history, literature, society and structural/historical-language modules nevertheless repeatedly teach a specific Dutch source corpus and its historical/institutional relationships. Most corresponding UCR teaching studies wider/global or other-regional corpora; hypothetical national project topics do not create the untaught continuing national progression. The conclusion follows this programme-level taught-substance test, with no language-only veto, title requirement or course-count threshold.
academicJudgment.narrowCoreTest: Removing proficiency, thesis and the disputed concentration leaves the known Dutch histories, literary histories/poetry/prose, national-society/film inquiry and structural/historical linguistics. Removing those too would discard the defining known academic object. A positive comparison limited only to general interpretation, philosophy or digital tools would therefore be misleading for this target.

readerValues.programmeDescription: Leiden’s Dutch Studies degree is designed for non-native speakers of Dutch. It develops advanced Dutch language skills alongside the literature, history, art and society of the Netherlands, culminating in a supervised thesis normally written in Dutch.
readerValues.comparisonExplanation: No close UCR comparison was found for the documented Dutch Studies curriculum. UCR offers Dutch-language foundations, cultural comparison and substantial literary, artistic, film and language-research methods. Its strongest combinations do not sustain the programme’s continuing study of Dutch history, literature, society and structural and historical language. The 170 EC shown include distinct first-year philosophy and second-year digital-humanities courses. The disputed concentration credits and complete progression remain unverified.

curriculum.limitation: Supported subset: 170 of 180 EC. The current catalogue now distinguishes first-year Philosophy of Science from second-year Humanities in a Digital World. The third-year concentration allocation and complete entrant timetable/progression still need confirmation.

componentNotes.dst1-04: Part of the first-semester beginner language course. Students enrol in the zero-credit language class and its three credited writing/grammar, reading/vocabulary and speaking/listening examinations together; the class adds no extra credits.
componentNotes.dst1-05: Taken with the beginner writing/grammar and speaking/listening components, rather than as a standalone examination.
componentNotes.dst1-06: Taken with the beginner writing/grammar and reading/vocabulary components, rather than as a standalone examination.
componentNotes.dst1-09: Writing begins from approximately A2 Dutch. Reading/Vocabulary 1B is taken in parallel unless the required level is already demonstrated.
componentNotes.dst1-10: Entry requires at least A2 reading proficiency in Dutch.
componentNotes.dst1-11: Speaking and listening begin from approximately A2 Dutch. Reading/Vocabulary 1B is taken in parallel unless the required level is already demonstrated.
componentNotes.dst1-08: Designed for non-native speakers with basic Dutch at approximately A2/B1. Successful completion also forms part of the programme’s first-year study-advice requirements.
componentNotes.dst2-01: The programme’s ordered progression requires a pass in Writing/Grammar 1B before this introduction to second-language acquisition.
componentNotes.dst2-02: Entry requires a pass in first-year Speaking/Listening 1B.
componentNotes.dst2-05: Entry requires a pass in first-year Writing/Grammar 1B.
componentNotes.dst2-06: Entry requires passes in first-year Writing/Grammar 1B and Reading/Vocabulary 1B.
componentNotes.dst2-07: Entry requires a pass in first-year Reading/Vocabulary 1B.
componentNotes.dst2-10: Entry requires a pass in Writing about Culture, Language Acquisition II.
componentNotes.dst3-5813valsy: Taken after all Language Acquisition II components. The 10 EC comprises 5 EC for independent reading and an oral examination, and 5 EC for processing academic literature in spoken and written Dutch. It prepares students for the thesis.
componentNotes.dst3-5813vscr3y: Entry requires completion of all first- and second-year components and Academic Reading and Writing, Language Acquisition III. Students conduct independent research with supervision, normally writing in Dutch on a language or culture topic. The compulsory thesis seminar has the same entry requirements and carries 0 EC. Participation, including presenting the research at the programme’s student symposium, is required for the thesis credits. The complete cohort timetable remains under review.
componentNotes.dst3-elective-space-30: 30 EC of a minor, approved courses, study abroad or an approved internship within the elective space. Courses must have sufficient level and avoid overlap with the required curriculum; Honours College courses cannot count. Recognized 30 EC minors at Leiden, Delft or Erasmus generally need no separate approval, subject to programme-specific overlap rules. An individual course package requires approval and normally allows at most 10 EC at level 100 and requires at least 10 EC at level 300 or above. Overlapping courses in the Second Language Acquisition or Digital Humanities and Artificial Intelligence minors require approved replacements.
